Thirty-day readmission was 15.8 percent after hospital at home and 13.1 percent after ward care; after adjustment, the difference was not clear (adjusted odds ratio 1.12, 95 percent CI 0.94 to 1.34). Readmission was higher after hospital at home for patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, and similar for other conditions. Patients who lived alone were more often readmitted in both groups. The study could not say why patients returned or whether returns were avoidable."},{"title":"Carers' experiences of acute care at home: responsibility, uncertainty and the decision to call","authors":"Varga-Achebe M, Sorensen-Tanaka L","year":2019,"venue":"Home Care Research Quarterly","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We spoke with 22 family carers of patients treated in a hospital-at-home service. Carers described taking on monitoring they did not feel trained for, especially at night, and uncertainty about when to call the team rather than an ambulance. Several described calling an ambulance because the service's night line felt slow or because they did not want to disturb the team. Carers who had a written plan for night-time worsening described fewer emergency calls. Carers with their own health problems or other caring duties described the most strain."},{"title":"Hospital at home for acute medical conditions: a systematic review of readmission and mortality","authors":"Petrov-Oduya S, Castellanos-Reid D, Mbeki-Holt K, Nakamura-Adu F","year":2023,"venue":"Health Services Evidence Reviews","doi":"10.5555/hser.2023.0144","providerType":"review","abstract":"We included 16 randomised trials and 21 observational studies of hospital at home for acute medical conditions. In trials, readmission within 90 days was similar to ward care (risk ratio 1.05, 95 percent CI 0.88 to 1.25) and mortality did not differ. Observational studies reported more variable readmission, with higher rates in services that took older and frailer patients. Few studies reported the reasons for readmission or the views of patients and carers. The trial populations were selected and may not reflect services that accept most referrals."},{"title":"Deciding to transfer back: clinicians' escalation decisions in hospital-at-home services","authors":"Laurent-Obi C, Haddad-Svensson R","year":2017,"venue":"Community Acute Medicine","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We held semi-structured conversations with 18 nurses and physicians working in three hospital-at-home services about decisions to transfer patients back to hospital. Clinicians described lower thresholds for transfer at night, when fewer staff were available to visit, and when they did not know the patient. Handovers between day and night teams often lacked a shared plan for worsening. Several described transfers that could have been avoided with a visit within two hours. Services with a named senior clinician on call described fewer night transfers."},{"title":"Reasons for readmission after hospital at home: a structured review of 300 readmissions","authors":"Achterberg-Ng R, Delacroix-Mwangi E, Fischer-Adeyemi O","year":2025,"venue":"Journal of Acute Care at Home","doi":"10.5555/jach.2025.0019","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"Two clinicians independently reviewed 300 consecutive readmissions within 30 days of discharge from a hospital-at-home service. The readmission was for the same condition in 41 percent, a fall in 22 percent, carer breakdown or social crisis in 18 percent and a new condition in the rest. Reviewers judged 34 percent of readmissions potentially avoidable, most often those after carer breakdown or night-time worsening. Agreement between reviewers on avoidability was moderate (kappa 0.58). Records rarely documented what patients and carers had understood about when to seek help."},{"title":"Information power and sample size in qualitative studies of care transitions","authors":"Brennan-Oyelowo T, Quist-Ferreira N","year":2020,"venue":"Qualitative Health Methods","doi":"10.5555/qhm.2020.0063","providerType":"journal-article","abstract":"We reviewed 64 qualitative studies of care transitions and the sample sizes they justified. Studies with a narrow aim, participants with specific experience of the transition and a strong analytic dialogue reported adequate information with 12 to 20 interviews per participant group. Studies that mixed patients, carers and clinicians in one sample needed larger totals to say anything about each group. We recommend stating the aim, the specificity of the sample and the analysis strategy before recruitment and revisiting the target during analysis rather than citing saturation alone."}]}
